nodes.name: Solid-state calcination of metal oxide precursors
nodes.procedure: RbSbWO6 was synthesized by solid-state calcination of the metal oxide precursors at a stoichiometric ratio of 1Rb:1Sb:1W. The precursors were mixed at the stoichiometric ratio and subjected to calcination to form the final white powder product with elemental composition confirmed by ICP-MS measurements.

unit_operations.name: Calcination
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: solid-state calcination of the metal oxide precursors at a stoichiometric ratio

nodes.source_text: we synthesized RbSbWO6 by solid-state calcination of the MO precursors at a stoichiometric ratio. Details of the synthesis, characterization, and electrochemical testing can be found in the Supporting Information. The physicochemical properties of the prepared white powder were determined by using various techniques. Inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) measurements reveal an elemental ratio of approximately 1Rb:1Sb:1W, consistent with the theoretical stoichiometry.

nodes.description: HER performance in 0.5 M H2SO4 acidic electrolyte
nodes.source_text: The catalyst was mixed with a conductive additive (carbon black, Vulcan XC-72R) at a mass ratio of 4:1 and loaded on a glassy carbon electrode (0.2 cm²) at 0.5 mgcm⁻² (metal oxide basis). The catalyst was precycled at 50 mV s⁻¹ between 0.1 and -0.6 V_RHE and 1 and 1.6 V_RHE for HER and OER, respectively, before their linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves were collected at a rotation rate of 1600 rpm at 5 mV s⁻¹. In the 0.5 M H₂SO₄ electrolyte (Figure 5a), the catalyst requires an overpotential (η₁₀) of 177 mV for the HER. Tafel analysis (Figure S7) has revealed HER Tafel slopes of 70 and 52 mVdec⁻¹ in the acidic and alkaline electrolytes, respectively. Though RbSbWO₆ exhibits a bit slower kinetics in the acidic electrolyte, its exchange current density (j₀) is about 18 times greater than that in the alkaline electrolyte. Its potential increased by 18 mV (Figure 5d) for HER in 0.5 M H₂SO₄ after 24 h tests. Further extending the test to 120 h could result in more obvious stability differences in the acidic and alkaline conditions. On the contrary, the potential only increases by 39 mV after 120 h under 0.5 M H₂SO₄ conditions for HER. While its HER and OER curves in the acid are almost identical, with only increments of 6 and 15 mV, respectively.

nodes.description: OER performance in 0.5 M H2SO4 acidic electrolyte
nodes.source_text: In the 0.5 M H₂SO₄ electrolyte (Figure 5a), the catalyst requires an overpotential (η₁₀) of 177 mV for the HER and 536 mV for the OER to reach a current density of 10 mA cm⁻². The stability of the RbSbWO₆ catalyst was further assessed by chronopotentiometry tests performed at 10 mAcm⁻² in 0.5 M H₂SO₄ and 1 M KOH electrolytes. Its potential increased by 33 mV (Figure 5c) and 18 mV (Figure 5d) for OER and HER in 0.5 M H₂SO₄ respectively. Further extending the test to 120 h could result in more obvious stability differences in the acidic and alkaline conditions. On the contrary, the potential only increases by 89 mV after 120 h under 0.5 M H₂SO₄ conditions for OER. While its HER and OER curves in the acid are almost identical, with only increments of 6 and 15 mV, respectively.

nodes.description: HER performance in 1 M KOH alkaline electrolyte
nodes.source_text: When subjected to a 1 M KOH electrolyte (Figure 5b), it exhibits improved OER performance, with the η₁₀ for the OER reduced by 113 - 423 mV. However, the η₁₀ for the HER has increased to 205 mV. Tafel analysis (Figure S7) has revealed HER Tafel slopes of 70 and 52 mVdec⁻¹ in the acidic and alkaline electrolytes, respectively. Its potential increased by 74 mV (Figure 5d) for HER in 1 M KOH after 24 h tests. The HER potential has dropped by 212 mV in KOH, much greater than the 39 mV for HER in acid. RbSbWO₆ shows a more significant performance drop in alkaline with substantial increments of 80 and 111 mV for HER and OER, respectively.

nodes.description: OER performance in 1 M KOH alkaline electrolyte
nodes.source_text: When subjected to a 1 M KOH electrolyte (Figure 5b), it exhibits improved OER performance, with the η₁₀ for the OER reduced by 113 - 423 mV. Its potential increased by 132 mV (Figure 5c) for OER in 1 M KOH after 24 h tests. Moreover, the catalyst also deactivates quickly for OER in 1 M KOH. The potential could reach 2 V after ∼94 h. RbSbWO₆ shows a more significant performance drop in alkaline with substantial increments of 80 and 111 mV for HER and OER, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD pattern confirms formation of RbSbWO6 with diffraction peaks assigned to various reflections from the simulated model. Average grain size of 58.2 nm calculated from Scherrer equation based on (311) plane.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Its X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern is displayed in Figure 4a. Diffraction peaks can be assigned to various reflections calculated from the simulated model, confirming the formation of RbSbWO6. The average grain size is about 58.2 nm, as calculated by the Scherrer equation based on the full width at half-maximum (fwhm) of its (311) plane.

nodes.evidence_snippet: The Raman spectrum (Figure 4b) of the samples shows representative chemical bond vibrations, similar to an earlier report. Different vibration modes can be assigned, including Rb-coupled Sb/WO6 bending (δRb-Sb/WO6) at 171 cm⁻¹, Sb/WO6 bending (δSb/WO6) at 350 and 451 cm⁻¹, and Sb/WO6 stretching (νSb/WO6) at 506 cm⁻¹.

nodes.characterization_summary: High-resolution HAADF-STEM images show clear lattice fringes with identification of (311), (240), and (400) planes. The (011) plane used for DFT calculations is orthogonal to the identified (400) plane, suggesting exposure of the (011) plane for electrochemical reactions.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The high-resolution high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscope (HAADF-STEM) images of the RbSbWO6 are shown in Figure 4c,d, where clear lattice fringes can be observed. At a higher resolution (Figure 4d), clear lattices of (311), (240), and (400) can be identified. Specifically, the (011) plane used for DFT calculations is orthogonal to the identified (400) plane, suggesting exposure of the (011) plane for electrochemical reactions.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS confirms elemental composition and oxidation states: W⁶⁺ at 36.0 and 37.8 eV (W 4f7/2 and 4f5/2), Rb⁺ at 111 and 112.5 eV (Rb 4d5/2 and 4d3/2), Sb⁵⁺ at 530.6 and 539.7 eV (Sb 3d5/2 and 3d3/2), and lattice oxygen at 532 eV (O 1s).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The W 4f7/2 and W 4f5/2 characteristic peaks are identified at 36.0 and 37.8 eV, respectively, corresponding to the W⁶⁺. The Rb 4d5/2 and 4d3/2 peaks are located at approximately 111 and 112.5 eV, respectively, with a separation of about 1.5 eV, corresponding to Rb⁺. Deconvolution of the Sb 3d spectrum revealed an Sb 3d5/2 peak at 530.6 eV and an Sb 3d3/2 peak at 539.7 eV, consistent with the presence of Sb⁵⁺. The O 1s spectrum shows a single peak at 532 eV, attributed to the lattice oxygen.

nodes.characterization_summary: Chronopotentiometric stability test at 10 mA/cm² shows superior stability in acidic electrolyte: potential increased by 33 mV (OER) and 18 mV (HER) in 0.5 M H₂SO₄ after 24 h, compared to 132 mV (OER) and 74 mV (HER) in 1 M KOH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The stability of the RbSbWO6 catalyst was further assessed by chronopotentiometry tests performed at 10 mAcm⁻² in 0.5 M H₂SO₄ and 1 M KOH electrolytes. Its potential increased by 33 mV (Figure 5c) and 18 mV (Figure 5d) for OER and HER in 0.5 M H₂SO₄ respectively, lower than 132 mV (Figure 5c) and 74 mV (Figure 5d) in 1 M KOH, after 24 h tests.

properties.description: Comparison of electrochemical performance before and after stability testing

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-electrolysis XRD shows structural features of RbSbWO6 maintained after acidic testing. Full width at half-maximum (fwhm) of (311) peak remains unchanged in acid but increased by 5.5-5.9% after alkaline testing, indicating deteriorated crystal structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: XRD patterns of the postelectrolysis samples are compared in Figure 6a. While the structural features of RbSbWO6 could be identified, their peak intensity exhibits varied changes. The full width at half-maximum (fwhm) of the (311) peak is calculated and further compared in the inset of Figure 6a. It can be found that the fwhm of the catalyst tested in acid remains the same as that of the pristine catalyst; it has increased significantly by about 5.5 and 5.9% after testing in 1 M KOH, showing a deteriorated crystal structure due to the surface reconstruction.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-electrolysis Raman shows emergence of weak features at 490 and 805-815 cm⁻¹ in alkaline-tested catalyst, assigned to σSb-O vibration of [SbO₆] octahedra in SbOₓ and νO-W-O vibration in WOₓ phases, indicating surface reconstruction in alkaline conditions.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Raman measurement also reveals the emergence of weak features at about 490 and 805 - 815 cm⁻¹ in the catalyst tested in the alkaline condition. These peaks can be assigned to the σSb-O vibration of [SbO6] octahedra in SbOx (e.g., Sb2O3 and Sb2O5) and the υO-W-O vibration in WOx phases formed in the surface reconstruction.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-electrolysis STEM-EDX shows uniform elemental distribution and maintained crystal structure after acidic testing with thin surface layer (<1 nm). After alkaline testing, dense amorphous surface layer forms with lower Rb and Sb signals and enriched W content.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 6a,b shows the postelectrolysis catalysts obtained under acidic conditions. After both the HER and the OER tests, the crystal structure of the catalysts could be well-maintained, except for the formation of a thin surface layer (less than 1 nm) with a slightly distorted structure. On the contrary, a much denser amorphous surface can be found from the sample tested under alkaline conditions, while obvious lattice fringes can be maintained in the core.

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP-OES measurements of post-test electrolytes show negligible metal leaching (<0.1 at.%) in acidic electrolyte after HER and OER tests. In alkaline electrolyte, Rb loss of 1.71-2.64 at.% and Sb loss of 1.08-1.70 at.% detected.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Rb, Sb, and W concentrations in the post-test electrolytes were assessed by ICP-OES measurements. The results listed in Table S9 suggest negligible metal leaching (<0.1 at. %) in the acidic electrolyte after both the HER and OER tests. On the contrary, a Rb loss of 1.71–2.64 at. % and an Sb loss of 1.08–1.70 at. % have been identified in the alkaline electrolyte.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-electrolysis XPS shows identical Sb 4d-W 4f spectra after acidic testing compared to pristine catalyst. After alkaline testing, intensity ratio of Sb 4d₅/₂ to W 4f₇/₂ dropped from 0.27 to 0.18-0.16, and Sb 4d peak redshifted by 0.1 eV, indicating reduced Sb valence state in amorphous surface layer.
nodes.evidence_snippet: After testing in acid, the spectra in the Sb 4d-W 4f region (Figure 7a) are identical to that of the pristine RbSbWO6 (Figure 4f). On the contrary, due to the catalyst surface reconstruction in the alkaline electrolyte, the intensity ratio between the Sb 4d5/2 to the W 4f7/2 has dropped significantly from about 0.27 in the pristine and acid-tested to about 0.18 and 0.16 after HER and OER tests in 1 M KOH, respectively.

properties.description: Weight loss feature

nodes.characterization_summary: Synchrotron X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) at Sb L₃ edge shows identical spectra in PFY mode before and after acidic testing. After alkaline testing, Sb features blueshift and intensify slightly with weak shoulder at 4142.3 eV indicating formation of low-valence Sb³⁺ species in reconstructed surface. W L₃ features show negligible position changes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: All spectra exhibit a predominant pre-edge peak and a white line peak at about 4134.5 and 4146.7 eV, corresponding to the electron transition from Sb 2p₃/₂ to 5s σ* and 5d orbitals, respectively. Similar to the XPS results, the Sb features in the catalysts tested in acid are identical with those in the pristine catalyst. After testing under alkaline conditions, both peaks have blueshifted and intensified slightly. Meanwhile, a weak shoulder at about 4142.3 eV is also noticed in the first-order derivative of the spectra (dμ(E)/dE, Figure 7e), confirming the formation of low-valence Sb species, e.g., Sb³⁺, in the reconstructed surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: Electron paramagnetic resonance spectra display catalyst lattice defect-induced feature at g = 2.003. Intensity remained stable but exhibited quick increments after biasing at -0.1 V_RHE in both acidic and alkaline electrolytes, suggesting formation of additional surface defects such as oxygen vacancies.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The EPR spectra (Figure S11) all display a catalyst lattice defect-induced feature at g = 2.003. The intensity of this feature remained stable but exhibited quick intensity increments of this feature after biasing at -0.1 V_RHE in both acidic and alkaline electrolytes, suggesting the formation of additional surface defects, e.g., Ov.

nodes.characterization_summary: Operando Raman spectra under OER conditions collected at 1.23, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, and 1.7 V_RHE show emergence of new feature at ~774 cm⁻¹ after biasing at potentials ≥1.4 V_RHE, assigned to stretching of surface adsorbed O* on W site (ν_W-O). Gradually increased intensity at higher applied potential indicates increasing O* coverage.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The catalyst surface state under OER conditions was further probed by operando Raman spectra collected at 1.23, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, and 1.7 V_RHE (Figure S12). After biasing at potentials greater than 1.4 V_RHE, a new feature at ~ 774 cm⁻¹ has emerged, which can be assigned to the stretching of the surface adsorbed O* on the W site (ν_W-O). Its gradually increased intensity at a higher applied potential is indicative of the increasing O* coverage, showing good agreement with our calculation results displayed in Figure 3c,e, where the W site in the O*-covered structure A is the most active OER site.

nodes.characterization_summary: Electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) measurements show negligible changes (0.45% and -0.02% for HER and OER, respectively) after acidic testing. Substantial ECSA increments of 10.76% and 12.41% found after alkaline testing, agreeing with metal leaching observations.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Different changes in the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) (Figure S9) are also spotted. Compared to the pristine catalysts, the ECSA of the catalyst after testing in the acidic electrolyte exhibits negligible changes (0.45 and -0.02% for HER and OER, respectively; Table S10). On the contrary, substantial ECSA increments of 10.76 and 12.41% are found after testing in the alkaline electrolyte, agreeing with the obvious metal leaching found by ICP-MS measurement.
